result:
There is a strange magic to an airport at three in the morning. Outside of standard time, the terminal becomes a liminal space, a waiting room between who you were and where you are going. The frantic energy of the daytime rush has evaporated, leaving behind a quiet hum of fluorescent lights and the distant drone of a floor buffer. 

Here, societal norms gently dissolve. A businessman in a rumpled suit sleeps soundly across three hard plastic chairs, using his briefcase as a pillow. Nearby, a backpacker in worn boots sips lukewarm coffee, staring at a departure board flickering with destinations that sound like promises: Reykjavik, Tokyo, Buenos Aires. Nobody judges the person eating pizza for breakfast or the one having a glass of wine before sunrise. Time isn’t real here.

I love watching the faces of the few souls awake. We are all ghosts in transit, stripped of our daily routines, united by the shared limbo of a layover. For a few hours, we have no responsibilities other than waiting for a boarding group to be called. You can reinvent yourself in the span of a terminal walk. Nobody knows your name, your failures, or your history. You are just a traveler with a ticket.

Then, the first hints of dawn bleed through the massive glass windows, painting the tarmac in shades of bruised purple and gold. The coffee shops rattle open their gates. The spell breaks, the world restarts, and we scatter into the sky.
